title: Useful work
hook: William Morris: useful work carries hope; useless toil does not (1884)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was John Ruskin, and the crooked stone leaf. Your line was a free mind at the chisel. Today, a designer with a test for any kind of work.

All work is good. Hard work is its own reward. Keep busy. Lines like these can sound like wisdom. William Morris, an English designer, craftsman and writer, wasn't so sure. In a lecture called Useful Work versus Useless Toil, he pointed out that the people most eager to praise all labor were often the ones living on someone else's. Then he drew a line through the middle of the word work. On one side, work worth doing. On the other, toil that only wears a person down. Today's word is the side he wanted: useful work.
screen: `ALL WORK IS GOOD?` → `MORRIS ISN'T SURE.` → `A LINE THROUGH THE WORD.`

segments.voice: First, his test. Morris says, in paraphrase, that worthwhile work carries hope in it, and useless toil carries none. So the question isn't whether you're busy. It's whether there's any hope in what you're doing. Second, he names three hopes. Hope of rest: that the work ends, and the rest is real. Hope of product: that what you make is worth having, useful or beautiful, not junk made to be thrown away. And hope of pleasure in the work itself: that the doing, not only the finishing, has something in it for the worker. In that third hope, a listener may hear an echo of Ruskin, yesterday. Third, what toil looks like: work with none of those hopes. Endless, so rest never comes. Pointless, so nothing good is made. Joyless, so the hours are only endured. Morris wanted a society to look hard at how much of its work fell on that side of the line, and to ask how much of it could be cut. Fourth, the small version. Morris wrote about whole economies, but his hopes fit inside a day: a to-do list can hold a report nobody reads, a form filled in twice. His lecture doesn't tell anyone to quit a job. It hands over a question to ask of any task: is there rest at the end of this, is the result worth having, and is there anything in the doing? If the answer is no, three times, maybe it can go.
screen: `HOPE, OR NO HOPE.` · `REST, PRODUCT, PLEASURE.` · `TOIL: ENDLESS, POINTLESS, JOYLESS.` · `THREE QUESTIONS FOR ANY TASK.` · then, large: `USEFUL WORK.`

segments.voice: Let this week's tasks pass one by one, like cards, and ask Morris's three questions lightly of each: rest at the end, a result worth having, anything in the doing? Notice the one task that fails all three, and hold it while you breathe, wondering whether it could be dropped, shrunk or handed back. If you pray, you can bring the choice into your own tradition's words.
Useful work. William Morris's name for work that carries hope: of rest, of a product worth having, and of pleasure in the doing. Today's word.
Your line: pleasure in the work itself. Busy isn't the test; hope is. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Morris's lecture Useful Work versus Useless Toil is read by students of design, craft and social thought, and his three hopes of rest, product and pleasure are cited in discussions of meaningful work.

notes: Morris paraphrased throughout (English original; not on the validator's list). The three hopes (rest, product, pleasure in the work itself) come from the lecture; confirm wording and order.
'The people most eager to praise all labor were often the ones living on someone else's' paraphrases Morris's opening argument; confirm faithfulness.
'Morris thought a society could be judged by how much of its work fell on that side of the line, and how much of it could be cut' is an interpretive summary; confirm.
Morris's link to Ruskin is stated as the listener hearing Ruskin's echo, not as a documented influence; Morris did acknowledge Ruskin elsewhere, which a scholar could add.
General claims about to-do lists softened to 'can carry'.
